sources.locator: HTML Living Standard; living standard accessed 2026-07; provisions applicable to Markup conformance
sources.claim: Conformance validation finds markup that violates HTML parsing or content-model requirements before browser recovery hides defects.

canonicalExplanation.summary: **Conformance** means your markup follows the HTML rules — valid nesting, allowed attributes, unique ids. Browsers silently repair broken markup, but each browser, screen reader and tool may repair it **differently**, so "looks fine in Chrome" proves little. Run a validator (like the W3C Nu checker), fix the **first** error first, and redesign structures the rules forbid rather than hoping repairs line up.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A course card is a big link, and inside it there's a "Save for later" button. It looks fine — but clicking the button sometimes follows the link, screen readers announce something odd, and the validator is shouting. A validator identifies a button nested inside a link, and the structure is redesigned instead of relying on browser repair. In this lesson you'll resolve all material conformance errors in a multi-page document set.

sections.heading: What counts as material

includes: Validate multi-page HTML and fix errors starting from the first.
Redesign forbidden structures such as interactive content nested in links.

outcomes: Resolve all material conformance errors in a multi-page document set.

examples.title: A button inside a link
examples.situation: A validator identifies a button nested inside a link, and the structure is redesigned instead of relying on browser repair.
walkthrough: **Validate:** the Nu checker reports "button must not appear as a descendant of a".
**Don't rely on browser repair:** Chrome and Firefox render it, but click and announcement behaviour differ.
**Redesign:** the card becomes an article with the heading link and the button as siblings; re-validate shows no errors.
examples.result: The card has one clear link and one independent button, and the structure is valid everywhere.

examples.title: The copy-pasted form with duplicate ids
examples.situation: Two newsletter forms on one page both use `id="email"`; the second label focuses the first input.
walkthrough: The validator reports a duplicate id.
`for="email"` can only point to the first element with that id.
Fix: `id="email-top"` and `id="email-footer"`, with matching for and aria-describedby references.
examples.result: Each label now focuses its own input, and the validator is clean.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: If a page looks correct in one browser, HTML conformance errors cannot matter.
misconceptions.correction: Browsers repair invalid markup silently and differently; assistive technologies and scripts then work from a different tree than you intended. Conforming markup gives every tool the same structure.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "A button inside a link", what behaviours differed between browsers?

analogy.example: Valid HTML is like **following traffic rules**: an illegal turn might work on a quiet day, but you're relying on every other driver to guess what you meant. Rules let everyone predict the same result.
limitations: Traffic rules are enforced by police; browsers never tell users about repairs.
One early wrong turn can cause a chain of problems — like cascading errors.

recap.summary: To resolve material conformance errors in a multi-page document set, validate every page, fix the first error first and re-validate, and redesign forbidden structures like interactive content inside links rather than relying on browser repair.
